params.title: Installation, Maintenance & Repair
params.subtitle: What each meter and test instrument measures and how it works, then the right way to measure, repair, install and troubleshoot.

onScreen: Meters and test instruments, then measuring, repairing, installing and troubleshooting
scenes.narration: Welcome to the technician's workbench. Electricity is invisible, so a radio technician relies on meters and test instruments to see what a circuit is doing. In this lesson you'll learn what each instrument measures, how it works inside, and which one to pick for each job. Then we'll cover the right way to test a receiver, repair a circuit board, install equipment and track down faults. You don't need any background in electronics: we'll refresh each basic idea just before we use it. By the end, you'll be ready for every question in this subelement, and you'll know why each answer is right. We'll start with what a meter actually measures.

params.title: What a meter measures
rows: How fast the flow does work

onScreen: Current: the flow of charge, in amperes
Power: volts times amps, in watts
scenes.narration: A meter measures electricity: a flow of tiny charged particles called electrons, moving through a conductor, a material they travel through easily, such as copper wire. Picture water in a pipe. Current is the flow itself: how much charge passes a point each second, measured in amperes, or amps. Voltage is the push that drives the flow, like water pressure, measured in volts. Resistance is whatever holds the flow back, like a narrow section of pipe, measured in ohms. Current only flows around a complete loop, called a circuit. And power, in watts, is how fast the flow delivers energy: volts times amps. The first meters in this lesson measure these quantities.

callouts.label: Selector: choose volts, amps or ohms, and the range
Common jack, plus a jack for volts or for amps
DMM: the reading appears as digits

onScreen: Selector: volts, amps or ohms, and the range
Common jack plus a volts or amps jack
scenes.narration: Volts, amps and ohms can all be measured with 1 instrument, the multimeter, the tool on every technician's bench. You turn the selector to choose what to measure and the range, which is the biggest value the meter will read on that setting. Then you touch the 2 probes to the circuit. One plugs into the common jack, or socket, and the other into the jack for what you're measuring. An older analog meter shows the reading with a needle swinging across a printed scale. A DMM, a digital multimeter, shows it as digits on a display. We'll start with the digital one, and a question the exam asks about its display.

marks.note: The most 3 full digits can show
3½ digits: leading ½ digit is only 0 or 1

marks.label: 2000 and up
marks.note: Won't fit: up a range, 1 digit less

onScreen: 3½ digits: the leading half digit shows only 0 or 1, so the meter counts to 1999
2000 and up won't fit: up a range, 1 digit less
Partial extended accuracy on the lower part of the range
scenes.narration: Many DMMs are sold as 3 and a half digit meters. What is a half digit? A full digit shows anything from 0 to 9, so 3 full digits stop at 999. A half digit is an extra leading digit that shows only 0 or 1, just 2 of the 10 values, so it counts as half. With it, the meter counts up to 1999. Readings that start with a 1 gain a digit of detail; a reading of 2000 won't fit, so the meter moves up a range and drops a digit. Extra detail, but only on the lower part: that's why the exam calls the half digit partial extended accuracy on the lower part of the range. It isn't a smaller readout on the left or right, and it does apply to DMMs.

params.title: Ohm's law
steps: I: current, in amperes; R: resistance, in ohms

onScreen: V in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms
scenes.narration: A digital meter hides its workings. An analog meter doesn't, and to understand it you need 1 rule: Ohm's law. It ties the 3 quantities together: V equals I times R. V is the voltage in volts, I is the current in amperes, and R is the resistance in ohms. In words, the push needed equals the flow times the opposition. Say 2 amperes flow through 6 ohms. 2 times 6 gives 12 volts across that resistance. That makes sense: more flow, or a narrower pipe, needs more push. Turned around, the same law gives the current: I equals V divided by R. We'll use both forms in this lesson.

params.title: Inside an analog meter: the movement

blocks.label: Coil between magnet poles
blocks.note: Current makes the coil a magnet

onScreen: A coil between magnet poles becomes a magnet
The needle swings: deflection, full scale at 50 µA
scenes.narration: With Ohm's law in hand, open up an analog meter. Inside is the meter movement, the part that turns current into needle motion. It's a coil of very fine wire on a pivot, between the poles of a permanent magnet. Current always creates magnetism, so current through the coil turns it into a magnet too. The 2 magnets push on each other, and the coil twists against a small spring. More current means more twist, and the needle fixed to the coil swings farther. How far it swings is called deflection. A sensitive movement reaches full-scale deflection, the end of the scale, with a tiny current, such as 50 microamperes, millionths of an ampere. And the coil's fine wire has some resistance of its own, called its internal resistance.

params.title: Voltage across a meter movement
steps: Movement: 50 µA full scale, 2,000 Ω inside
Half scale needs half the current: 25 µA
Check: full scale would take 0.1 volts

onScreen: 50 µA movement with 2,000 Ω internal resistance
scenes.narration: Because the coil has resistance, a current through it needs a voltage across it, and Ohm's law tells us how much. Here's the exam's example. A 50 microampere meter movement has an internal resistance of 2,000 ohms. What voltage gives half-scale deflection? Step 1: the needle's swing follows the current, so half scale needs half the full-scale current. Half of 50 microamperes is 25 microamperes. Step 2: V equals I times R, so 25 microamperes times 2,000 ohms. That's 25 millionths of an ampere times 2,000, which is 0.05 volts. Does it make sense? Full scale would take twice as much, 0.1 volts. So the answer is 0.05 volts, and the 0.10 volt choice is a trap: that's the full-scale figure.

blocks.label: Voltage to measure
blocks.note: Far more than the movement can take

blocks.label: Series multiplier resistor
blocks.note: Drops most of the applied voltage

onScreen: Series multiplier resistor drops most of it
The movement sees only a small share
scenes.narration: So on its own, our movement reads no more than 0.1 volts. How can it measure bigger voltages? Inside a voltmeter, a resistor is placed in series with the movement, meaning in the same path, one after the other. It's called a series multiplier resistor. The same current flows through both, and V equals I times R, so the bigger resistance takes the bigger share of the voltage. The multiplier's resistance is far higher, so it drops most of the applied voltage, like a long, narrow stretch of pipe that uses up most of the pressure. The movement gets only a small share. That's why a series multiplier is used to increase the voltage-indicating range of a voltmeter. It doesn't decrease the range, and it isn't used with an ammeter.

onScreen: Series multiplier: voltmeter, in series, drops most of the voltage
Shunt: ammeter, in parallel, carries most of the current
scenes.narration: That's the voltmeter. Now the ammeter, which measures current. You open the circuit and insert the ammeter, so all the current being measured flows through it. But our movement can carry only 50 microamperes. The answer is a shunt resistor: a low resistance connected in parallel with the movement, meaning side by side, giving the current a second path. Think of a wide bypass pipe beside a narrow one: most of the water takes the bypass. In the same way, the shunt carries most of the current, and only a small, fixed fraction goes through the movement. So a shunt resistor is used to increase the ampere-indicating range of an ammeter. The wrong choices swap these 2 parts. Remember: series multiplier for volts, parallel shunt for amps.

params.title: The logic probe
items: Digital circuits use just 2 voltage states: high and low
High stands for 1, low stands for 0
A logic probe touched to a point lights up for high or low
Ohmmeter, megger, signal strength meter: none show logic states

onScreen: Digital circuits: 2 voltage states, high and low
Logic probe: lights show high or low
Not an ohmmeter, megger or signal strength meter
scenes.narration: So far, a voltage or current could take any value. Digital circuits, the kind inside computers and modern radios, use just 2 voltage states: high and low. High stands for 1 and low for 0, and every number and command is built from those 1s and 0s. To check them, a technician uses a logic probe, a pen-shaped tester. Touch its tip to a point in the circuit, and its lights show whether that point is high or low, and often whether it's pulsing. The logic probe, then, is the instrument used to indicate high and low digital voltage states. The other choices can't: an ohmmeter measures resistance, a megger measures insulation resistance, and a signal strength meter reads radio signals in the air.

params.title: Transmitter to antenna: the feed line

blocks.label: Feed line (coax)
blocks.note: Carries the power to the antenna

blocks.label: Antenna
blocks.note: Sends it out, if well matched

onScreen: Transmitter sends RF power up the feed line
A well-matched antenna sends it out
A mismatch reflects some power back down the line
scenes.narration: 1 more meter, and it works between a transmitter and its antenna. Radio power, called RF, for radio frequency, travels from the transmitter up a cable called the feed line. It's usually coax: a center wire inside a tube-shaped shield. When the antenna suits the line electrically, which is called a good match, it accepts nearly all the power and sends it out as radio waves. When it doesn't, because the antenna is damaged or a cable or connector is faulty, part of the power bounces back down the line, like a wave off a sea wall. The outgoing and returning waves combine into a fixed pattern of high and low spots along the line, called standing waves. The worse the mismatch, the stronger they are.

marks.label: High SWR
marks.note: Check the antenna, cable and connectors

onScreen: SWR meter: compares forward and reflected power
High SWR: check the antenna, cable and connectors
scenes.narration: An SWR meter, short for standing wave ratio meter, measures those standing waves: the ratio is the high spots compared with the low spots. It sits in the feed line and compares the forward power with the reflected power. A perfect match reads 1 to 1, meaning nothing comes back. A low SWR shows a good match, so the antenna and line are working properly. A high or changing reading points to a damaged antenna, connector or cable. That's why an SWR meter may be used to verify proper radio antenna functioning. An ohmmeter, a frequency meter or a different radio can't tell you that.

params.title: Frequency and time
labels: 1 cycle: 1 complete back-and-forth
Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz
Period: the time 1 cycle takes
Frequency = 1 ÷ period

onScreen: Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz
scenes.narration: That's the meters. The next group of test equipment deals with frequency and time. We met the word in RF, radio frequency, so what is a frequency? Alternating current, and every radio signal, swings back and forth, over and over. 1 complete back-and-forth is called a cycle. Frequency is how many cycles happen each second, measured in hertz, and 1000 hertz is a kilohertz. The time 1 cycle takes is called the period. Frequency and period are reciprocals: each is 1 divided by the other. If a signal makes 1000 cycles every second, each cycle lasts 1 thousandth of a second. Measure either one, and you know the other.

blocks.label: Counter
blocks.note: Counts cycles, or times the gap

onScreen: Counter counts cycles or times events
Display: frequency, or time between events
scenes.narration: A frequency counter puts those ideas to work. Inside, a counter counts the incoming signal's cycles. For how long? An accurate time base, an internal clock, sets an exact interval, such as 1 second. The number of cycles in that second is the frequency, and the display shows it. Or the counter can time the gap between 2 events, such as 2 pulses; for a repeating signal, that gap is the period. In the exam's words, a frequency counter is used to measure the time between events, or the frequency, which is the reciprocal of the time. Watch for the zero beat trap: tuning a variable oscillator, a circuit that makes a steady signal, until it matches the unknown one. That's an older kind of frequency meter, not a counter.

params.title: The frequency standard
items: A counter is only as accurate as its time base
Frequency standard: an extremely stable oscillator
It produces a highly accurate reference frequency
Used to calibrate counters, signal generators and transmitters

onScreen: A counter is only as accurate as its time base
Frequency standard: an extremely stable oscillator
Produces a highly accurate reference frequency
scenes.narration: That raises a question. A counter is only as accurate as its time base, so how do you know the time base is right? You compare it with a frequency standard: an extremely stable oscillator, like the master clock you set every other clock by. A frequency standard is a device used to produce a highly accurate reference frequency. Notice the difference: a counter measures an unknown frequency, while a standard produces a known one. Technicians use it to calibrate other equipment, meaning to check and adjust it against the reference: counters, transmitters, and signal generators, the instruments that make test radio signals. It isn't a frequency used for sending messages, and it isn't a measuring device.

params.title: Which standard in the field?
rows: The natural vibration of rubidium atoms
Compact, quick warm-up: the field choice
The natural vibration of cesium atoms
Large and costly: kept in labs

onScreen: Rubidium standard: compact, quick warm-up, far more stable than quartz
LC tank oscillator: drifts the most
scenes.narration: Frequency standards come in several kinds. A quartz crystal, the same part that keeps a wristwatch on time, is a sliver of quartz that vibrates at a precise rate, but it drifts, meaning it wanders slightly off frequency, with temperature and age. An atomic standard does better by locking onto the natural vibration of atoms. Which one do field technicians use as a time base standard? The rubidium standard. It's compact, it warms up quickly, and it's far more stable than quartz. A cesium beam standard is even more precise, but it's larger and costlier, so it usually stays in a laboratory. An LC tank oscillator drifts the most of all. It's a simple circuit of a coil, written L, and a capacitor, written C, a part that stores charge.

params.title: Why an AM radio hears electrical noise
labels: EMI: unwanted electrical noise
Modulation: sound placed on a radio wave
AM: the sound changes the wave's strength
Noise changes the strength too, so AM hears it

onScreen: Modulation: sound placed on a radio wave
AM: the sound changes the wave's strength
Noise changes the strength too, so an AM radio hears it
scenes.narration: Frequency tools done, now a hunting job, and it starts with interference. EMI, electromagnetic interference, is unwanted electrical noise. Motors, switching power supplies like the ones that charge computers, and sparking switch contacts all give it off, and radios pick it up as buzzing or crackling. Why do some radios hear it so well? Modulation means placing sound onto a radio wave. In AM, amplitude modulation, the sound rides on changes in the wave's strength, which you can see in the rising and falling outline here. Electrical noise is also a jumble of sudden changes in strength, so an AM receiver turns it straight into sound you can hear.

blocks.label: Louder as you get closer
blocks.note: Follow the noise to its source

onScreen: Noise source: a motor, power supply or sparking contact
Portable AM receiver tuned between stations
The noise grows louder near the source
scenes.narration: That makes an AM radio a handy noise detector. Aboard a ship or an aircraft, how do you find where EMI is coming from? Use a portable AM receiver. Tune it between stations, so all you hear is noise, and carry it around. The noise grows louder as you approach the source, like a game of hotter and colder. A multimeter, a logic probe, or the oscilloscope we'll meet soon all need a direct connection to a circuit, so none of them can find a source that sends its noise through the air.

params.title: Analog wattmeter accuracy
steps: A wattmeter reads power, in watts
Full scale on this range: 100 W
params.answer: ±5 W at every reading on the scale

onScreen: Accuracy is stated as a percent of full scale
The same ±5 W applies at every reading
scenes.narration: Back on the bench, a meter for power: the wattmeter, which measures power in watts, such as the RF power a transmitter sends to its antenna. On an analog wattmeter, the maker states the accuracy as a percentage of full scale, the top of the scale. Take a meter rated plus or minus 5 percent on its 100 watt scale. 5 percent of 100 watts is 5 watts, so the needle can be off by up to 5 watts either way. Here's the catch: that 5 watts isn't a percentage of what you're reading. It's a fixed amount, and it applies at every point on the scale, whether the needle shows 100 watts or 20.

params.title: Only the upper third is truly calibrated

onScreen: At 20 W, ±5 W is 25% of the reading
Upper 1/3 of the scale: the only truly calibrated part
scenes.narration: So what does a fixed 5 watts do at different readings? At full scale, 5 watts out of 100 is just 5 percent. But at a 20 watt reading, 5 watts divided by 20 watts is 25 percent of the reading, far too rough to trust. Only near the top is the error small. That's the exam answer: the accuracy is only at full scale, and that absolute number, the fixed 5 watts, is carried through to the rest of the range, so the upper third of the meter is the only truly calibrated part. The traps say the accuracy is constant everywhere, holds only in the top 5 percent, or can't be determined. For a trustworthy reading, pick a scale that puts the needle in its upper third.

params.title: What SINAD means
rows: Receiver audio with the test tone
The 1st reading compared with the 2nd, in dB

onScreen: With the tone: signal + noise + distortion
SINAD: the ratio of the 2, in decibels
scenes.narration: The next instrument tests receivers, and its name needs unpacking first. Feed a receiver a radio signal carrying a steady 1000 hertz test tone, and its audio output holds 3 things: the tone, which is the wanted signal; noise, the background hiss; and distortion, unwanted tones the receiver adds by not reproducing the signal perfectly. SINAD stands for signal plus noise and distortion, compared with noise and distortion alone. If the noise and distortion are tiny, the first reading is far bigger than the second. To compare 2 levels like these, technicians use decibels, written dB: a scale where every 3 decibels roughly doubles the power. So the higher the SINAD in decibels, the cleaner the audio.

blocks.label: 1000 Hz bandstop filter
blocks.note: Sharp and internal: notches out the tone

onScreen: Multirange AF voltmeter calibrated in dB
scenes.narration: A SINAD meter makes that measurement. The receiver's audio can pass through a sharp, internal 1000 hertz bandstop filter, which blocks 1 narrow band of frequencies, here the test tone. Next comes a multirange AF voltmeter, AF meaning audio frequency, calibrated in decibels. With the filter out, it reads the whole audio. With the filter in, it reads only the noise and distortion left over. Comparing the 2 readings gives the SINAD. Used together, the filter and voltmeter perform quieting tests: with no signal, many receivers hiss loudly, and the test shows how much an incoming signal quiets that hiss. Filter plus voltmeter: that's the SINAD meter the exam describes. A reflectometer, a dip meter and a vector-impedance meter test antennas, cables and circuits, not receiver audio.

callouts.label: The screen is a graph: voltage up and down, time across
The trace: a bright line sweeping left to right
Time base: sets the sweep speed, in time per division

onScreen: Screen: a graph, voltage up and time across, divided into squares
Trace: a bright line sweeping left to right
Time base: sets the sweep speed, in time per division
scenes.narration: Now the oscilloscope. Our other instruments give a single number; an oscilloscope, or scope for short, draws a picture. Its screen is a graph: up and down is voltage, and left to right is time. A grid divides it into squares called divisions. A bright line, the trace, sweeps across the screen from left to right at a steady speed, then jumps back and starts again. A circuit called the sweep oscillator drives it, and the time base control sets its speed, in time per division. On a scope, time base just means this sweep timing, not the counter's clock.

callouts.label: The signal enters at the input
Vertical amplifier: moves the trace up and down, in volts per division
Across and up and down together: the waveform

onScreen: The signal enters at the input
Vertical amplifier: moves the trace up and down, in volts per division
scenes.narration: That's the side-to-side motion. The up-and-down motion comes from the signal itself. The probe touches the circuit, and the signal enters the scope's input. From there it goes through the vertical amplifier. An amplifier is a circuit that makes a signal bigger, and this one pushes the trace up and down in step with the voltage. The volts per division control sets how many volts each square stands for. Put the 2 motions together, steady across and following the voltage up and down, and the trace draws the signal's waveform: its shape, drawn over time.

onScreen: Scope: the wave over time; analyzer: strength at each frequency
Both show audio or radio signals
scenes.narration: Because it plots against time, we say an oscilloscope displays electrical signals in the time domain. Another instrument, the spectrum analyzer, shows the same signals a different way: in the frequency domain. Instead of a wave wiggling over time, it shows how strong the signal is at each frequency. Think of music. A scope is like watching a guitar string vibrate, moment by moment. A spectrum analyzer is like the bouncing bars on a stereo's display, 1 bar for each pitch. That's the difference the exam asks about: scope, time domain; analyzer, frequency domain. The traps reverse them, or claim one is only for audio and the other only for radio. Both can show audio or radio signals, within their limits.

params.title: What an oscilloscope can measure
items: Electrical voltage, read straight off the screen
Electron flow (current), with the aid of a resistor: I = V ÷ R
The phase difference between 2 signals
Not a scope job: measuring the velocity of light with an LED

onScreen: Not: velocity of light with an LED
scenes.narration: So what can a scope measure? Electrical voltage, directly: count how many divisions the trace moves up and multiply by the volts per division. Electron flow, which is current, with the aid of a resistor: send the current through a known resistor, read the voltage across it, and Ohm's law gives the current, I equals V divided by R. And the phase difference between 2 signals. Phase is where a wave is in its cycle, so with 2 traces on the screen together, you can see how far one lags behind the other. What can't it do? Measure the velocity of light with the aid of an LED, a light emitting diode, a tiny electronic lamp. That's the exception the exam is looking for.

params.title: Loading: measuring changes the circuit
items: Every instrument draws a little current from the circuit
That changes the circuit: called loading
Like a tire gauge letting out a little air
A scope's input: 1 MΩ, which can still upset a sensitive circuit

onScreen: Every instrument draws a little current
Like a tire gauge letting out air
scenes.narration: Connecting a scope brings a problem. Any instrument draws a little current from the circuit it's measuring, and that changes what the circuit does. That's called loading. It's like checking a tire with a pressure gauge, which lets out a little air as it measures. The less current the instrument draws, the less it disturbs the circuit. A scope's input has a resistance of 1 megohm, 1 million ohms. By Ohm's law, a high resistance draws only a small current, but even that can upset a sensitive circuit.

params.title: The 10:1 divider probe
steps: 10:1 probe adds about 9 MΩ in series
Less loading: the circuit is disturbed less
Signal divided by 10: multiply the reading by 10

onScreen: 10:1 probe adds about 9 MΩ: the circuit sees about 10 MΩ
scenes.narration: The cure is a 10 to 1 divider probe. It places about 9 megohms in series with the scope's 1 megohm, so the circuit sees about 10 megohms in all. By Ohm's law, 10 times the resistance draws a tenth of the current, so the circuit is disturbed far less. That's how a 10 to 1 divider probe decreases circuit loading. The price: the 2 resistances divide the voltage too, so only a tenth of the signal reaches the scope, and you multiply the reading by 10. Dual input amplifiers, inductive probes and resistive probes are the wrong choices.

params.title: What sets a scope's frequency response

blocks.label: Vertical amplifier
blocks.note: Its bandwidth sets the highest frequency

blocks.label: Time base (sweep oscillator)
blocks.note: Only sets how fast the trace sweeps

onScreen: Vertical amplifier: sets the maximum frequency response
Time base: only sets the sweep speed
scenes.narration: Loading is 1 practical limit. Another is speed. A scope's frequency response is the range of frequencies it can display accurately. Above that, fast signals come out shrunken and rounded off. What sets the limit? Follow the signal: it enters through the probe, then must pass through the vertical amplifier on its way to the display. If that amplifier can't keep up with a fast signal, nothing after it can fix it. So the vertical amplifier determines the maximum frequency response of an oscilloscope. Its bandwidth, the range of frequencies it passes, becomes the scope's bandwidth. The time base, the horizontal sweep and the power supply are the trap answers: the time base only sets how fast the trace sweeps across.

params.title: What limits accuracy and stability
items: Sweep oscillator quality: an even, steady sweep keeps time readings accurate
A poor sweep makes the picture jitter
Deflection amplifier bandwidth: how faithfully fast signals are drawn
Exam answer: sweep oscillator quality and deflection amplifier bandwidth

onScreen: Answer: sweep oscillator quality and deflection amplifier bandwidth
scenes.narration: The exam also asks about a scope's accuracy, frequency response and stability together. What limits all 3? 2 things. First, the quality of the sweep oscillator. Time is read from how far the trace has moved across, so the sweep must be perfectly even and steady. A poor sweep oscillator throws off time readings and makes the picture jitter. Second, the bandwidth of the deflection amplifiers, the amplifiers that move the trace, including the vertical amplifier. Their bandwidth decides how faithfully fast waveforms are reproduced. The exam answer: sweep oscillator quality and deflection amplifier bandwidth. Choices about tube face voltage increments or output impedance sound technical, but they're wrong.

params.title: Refresher: single sideband
labels: Carrier: a steady radio wave, suppressed in SSB
Upper sideband: carries the voice
Lower sideband: removed

scenes.narration: 1 more job for the scope involves a kind of transmission you need to picture first. A transmitter puts out a carrier, a steady radio wave at its operating frequency. In AM, the voice changes the carrier's strength, and that creates sidebands, copies of the voice just above and just below the carrier's frequency. The carrier itself carries no voice at all, and each sideband carries all of it. So SSB, single sideband, sends just 1 sideband and suppresses the carrier and the other sideband. That saves power and takes up half the room on the band. It also means an SSB transmitter puts out almost nothing until you speak, and its output rises and falls with your voice. Hold onto that; it comes back in troubleshooting.

params.title: Checking SSB signal quality
labels: The oscilloscope shows the shape of the SSB waveform
2-tone test: smooth, regular loops mean a clean signal
Flat tops or uneven loops: distortion

onScreen: Oscilloscope: shows the shape of the SSB waveform
scenes.narration: How do you check the signal quality of an SSB transmission? With an oscilloscope, because it shows the shape of the waveform. A common way is the 2-tone test: feed 2 steady audio tones into the microphone input and look at the transmitter's output on the scope. 2 tones together make a steady, repeating pattern that's easy to judge. A clean transmitter draws regular, smooth, rounded loops like these. If the tops are squashed flat, the transmitter is being overdriven, pushed harder than it can handle, and it distorts. A leaking carrier changes the pattern too. The other choices, a field strength meter, a signal level meter or a sidetone monitor, can't show the waveform's shape. So for SSB signal quality, use the oscilloscope.

blocks.label: Pulse generator
blocks.note: Sends a sharp pulse down the line

blocks.label: Fault
blocks.note: Reflects part of the pulse back

onScreen: Oscilloscope: the reflection delay gives the distance
scenes.narration: Some jobs call for specialized instruments, and the first combines 2 we already know. Remember how a mismatch reflects power back down a feed line? Any transmission line, the general name for a cable that carries signals, also reflects at a fault: a break, a crushed spot, a wet connector, or 2 wires touching. Put a pulse generator, which makes short bursts of voltage, together with an oscilloscope, and you have a TDR, a time-domain reflectometer, used to measure the characteristics of transmission lines. It sends a sharp pulse down the line. At a fault, part of the pulse bounces back, like an echo from a canyon wall, and the scope shows when it arrives. The pulse travels at a known speed, so the longer the delay, the farther away the fault.

params.title: Time domain or frequency domain reflectometer?
rows: A signal swept across the band
Showing the match at each frequency

onScreen: TDR: 1 sharp pulse, finds where a fault is
Frequency domain reflectometer: sweeps the operating band
Most accurate for antennas and lines at the operating frequency
scenes.narration: The TDR has a cousin with a similar name, and the exam likes to swap them. A TDR's sharp pulse is great for finding where a fault is, but an antenna behaves differently at different frequencies, and a single pulse can't show that. A frequency domain reflectometer instead sweeps a test signal across the antenna's actual operating band, the range of frequencies it's used on, and measures the reflections at each frequency. It shows the match right where the antenna will be used, plus the distance to faults. The exam's answer, then: the frequency domain reflectometer is the most accurate instrument for checking antennas and transmission lines at the antenna's operating frequency. Not the time domain reflectometer, a wattmeter or a DMM.

params.title: Reading a spectrum analyzer
labels: Horizontal axis: frequency
Vertical axis: amplitude
Each signal: a peak at its own frequency

onScreen: Each signal stands at its own frequency
scenes.narration: Back to the spectrum analyzer we met beside the scope. Here it shows an AM signal. Read the axes first. The horizontal axis displays frequency, low on the left, high on the right. The vertical axis displays amplitude, the strength of each signal. So every signal stands at its own frequency, with a height that shows how strong it is. You can see the tall carrier in the middle and a sideband on each side, just as we described for AM. On the exam: horizontal is frequency, vertical is amplitude. Don't mix it up with a scope, whose horizontal axis is time.

params.title: Spurious signals on a spectrum analyzer

onScreen: A spectrum analyzer shows each one; a wattmeter reads only total power
scenes.narration: That view makes the spectrum analyzer ideal for a key transmitter test. A transmitter should send only its wanted signal. Anything it puts out on other frequencies is a spurious signal, and it can interfere with other radio services. Common ones are harmonics: copies at 2 and 3 times the operating frequency. On a spectrum analyzer, each spurious signal stands out as its own small peak, and you can measure its strength. That makes a spectrum analyzer the test instrument that can display spurious signals in the output of a radio transmitter. A wattmeter can't: it reads only the total power, so the spurious signals hide inside 1 number. A logic analyzer, which watches digital circuits, and a TDR, which tests cables, are wrong too.

params.title: The service monitor: a test bench in a box
items: Monitors a transmitter's frequency and modulation
Signal generator: feeds test signals to a receiver
Checks receiver sensitivity and distortion
Generates audio tones

scenes.narration: For everyday radio servicing, carrying a separate instrument for every test would be a chore. So radio service technicians commonly use a service monitor, also called a communications test set. It combines several instruments in 1 box. It monitors a transmitter's frequency and modulation. Its built-in signal generator feeds test signals to a receiver. With its SINAD and distortion meter, it checks receiver sensitivity and distortion. And it generates audio tones for testing. That's the answer when the exam lists all of those jobs together. An oscilloscope, a spectrum analyzer or a DMM handles only part of the list.

blocks.label: Signal generator
blocks.note: RF signal with a 1000 Hz tone

onScreen: Signal generator: RF signal with a 1000 Hz tone
SINAD meter measures the recovered audio
scenes.narration: With the instruments in hand, we turn to measurement procedures, the standard ways of testing. First, receiver sensitivity: the weakest signal a receiver can turn into usable audio. A more sensitive receiver hears weaker, more distant stations. To measure it, a signal generator feeds the receiver an RF signal at a chosen strength, carrying the 1000 hertz test tone. The receiver recovers the audio, meaning it takes the tone back off the radio signal, and that recovered audio goes to the SINAD meter. Now turn the generator's level down. As the signal gets weaker, noise creeps in and the SINAD falls. The question is where to stop.

params.title: Sensitivity: 12 dB of SINAD
items: Exact sensitivity: measure the recovered audio for 12 dB of SINAD
The weakest RF level that still gives 12 dB of SINAD
About 25% noise and distortion: speech still understandable
Traps: 10 dB of SINAD, 10 dB or 25 dB of quieting

onScreen: Sensitivity: measure the recovered audio for 12 dB of SINAD
The weakest RF level giving 12 dB of SINAD
Not 10 dB of SINAD, nor 10 or 25 dB of quieting
scenes.narration: Everyone agrees on 1 stopping point. The exact sensitivity specification of a receiver is found by measuring the recovered audio for 12 decibels of SINAD. The sensitivity is the weakest RF level, usually given in microvolts, millionths of a volt, that still gives 12 decibels of SINAD. At that point the audio is about 25 percent noise and distortion: rough, but speech is still understandable. Because the whole industry uses the same point, you can fairly compare 1 receiver with another. Watch the numbers in the traps: 10 decibels of SINAD, and 10 or 25 decibels of quieting. Quieting is an older, less precise method. Remember 12 decibels of SINAD.

params.title: FM and deviation
labels: FM: the voice shifts the carrier's frequency
A louder voice makes a wider swing
Deviation: how far the frequency swings, in kHz

onScreen: FM: the voice shifts the carrier's frequency
Deviation: how far the frequency swings
scenes.narration: The next measurements involve FM, frequency modulation, the system most 2-way radios use on VHF and UHF, the very high and ultra high frequency bands. In AM, the voice changes the carrier's strength. In FM, the voice shifts the carrier's frequency up and down instead, so the waves bunch together and spread apart, as you see here. A louder voice makes a wider swing. How far the frequency swings from its center is called deviation, measured in kilohertz. Each channel is like a lane on a highway, with a set width. Too much deviation makes the signal too wide for its lane, and it spills into the neighboring channel.

marks.label: 5.0 kHz
marks.note: Wideband VHF or UHF voice: the maximum

onScreen: 5.0 kHz: maximum on a normal wideband VHF or UHF channel
scenes.narration: So how wide may the swing be? On a normal wideband VHF or UHF channel, 25 kilohertz wide, the maximum FM deviation for voice is 5.0 kilohertz. Don't be fooled by 2.5 kilohertz. That's the figure for narrowband channels, which are only 12.5 kilohertz wide, so their swing is cut in half. And 7.5 or 10 kilohertz would be too wide for either. For a normal wideband channel, remember 5.0 kilohertz.

params.title: Modulation-acceptance bandwidth test
steps: 2. Set the RF level 6 dB above it
4. Stop when SINAD falls back to 12 dB
params.answer: That deviation shows the effective bandwidth

onScreen: RF level 6 dB above the 12 dB SINAD point
Raise the deviation until SINAD falls back to 12 dB
That deviation shows the effective bandwidth
scenes.narration: Deviation and SINAD come together in the next test. A receiver has filters that let in only so wide a signal. How wide a signal it can actually accept is its effective bandwidth, and a modulation-acceptance bandwidth test determines it. Step 1: find the 12 decibel SINAD point, as before. Step 2: set the RF level 6 decibels above it. That's 2 doublings, about 4 times the power, so signal strength can't be the problem. Step 3: slowly raise the deviation, making the signal wider. Step 4: once the signal is too wide for the receiver's filters, distortion rises and SINAD falls back to 12 decibels. Stop there: that deviation shows how wide a signal the receiver accepts. That's the purpose of the test: to determine the effective bandwidth of a communications receiver.

blocks.label: Scanner with P25 decoding
blocks.note: Turns the data back into voice

onScreen: P25: voice sent as digital data
Scanner with P25 decoding: voice heard
Without P25 decoding: only digital noise
scenes.narration: Many modern radios are digital, and that changes how you monitor and measure them. P25, short for Project 25, is a digital radio standard widely used by public safety agencies, such as police and fire services. A P25 radio turns the voice into digital data, a stream of 1s and 0s, before sending it. A scanner, a receiver that hunts through channels for activity, can monitor a P25 system, but only if it has P25 decoding, which turns that data back into voice. Without decoding, all it hears is a harsh digital buzz. So the answer is yes, if the scanner has P25 decoding. Not regardless of decoding, and there's no such thing as P26 decoding.

params.title: Measuring CDMA power
items: CDMA: many users share 1 channel, each with its own code
The signal is noise-like: its power changes constantly
An analog power meter can't follow it: the reading is not accurate
Use a power sensor designed for digital signals

onScreen: Use a sensor designed for digital signals
scenes.narration: Digital signals can fool power meters too. CDMA, code division multiple access, lets many users share the same channel at the same time, each spread out and tagged with its own code. Added together, the result looks like noise, with power that jumps up and down constantly, and brief peaks far above the average. An analog power meter, like the wattmeter we met earlier, is built for a steady carrier, so its needle can't follow, and the reading is not accurate. That's the true statement on the exam: the RF power reading on a CDMA radio is not accurate on an analog power meter. Power can still be measured, with a sensor designed for digital signals.

params.title: Words for the repair bench
items: Circuit board: copper tracks on a board join the parts
Solder: a soft mix of metals, melted to join parts to the board
Plated-through hole: a copper-lined hole joining both sides
Desoldering: removing old solder to free a part

onScreen: Circuit board: copper tracks join the parts
Solder: a soft mix of metals that melts low
Plated-through hole: copper-lined, joins both sides
scenes.narration: Now from measuring to fixing: repair procedures. A few words first. Most radio circuits are built on a circuit board, a stiff board with thin copper tracks that act as wires between the parts. Parts are fixed in place with solder, a soft mix of metals that melts at a low temperature. A soldering iron melts it, and it hardens into a joint that holds the part and conducts electricity. Many boards have plated-through holes, holes lined with copper that connect tracks on both sides of the board. To replace a part, you first remove the old solder, which is called desoldering. Each of these jobs has a right tool, and wrong ones that do damage.

blocks.label: Your body
blocks.note: Builds up static charge as you move

blocks.label: CMOS chip
blocks.note: A static spark can punch through it

onScreen: Your body builds up static charge
CMOS chips are easily damaged by a spark
A wrist strap bleeds the charge to ground
scenes.narration: Before you touch a board, think about static electricity. As you move, your body builds up electric charge, the same charge that snaps when you touch a doorknob. Some parts are easily damaged by it, above all CMOS chips, CMOS meaning complementary metal oxide semiconductor. Inside them are layers of insulation so thin that a static spark too small to feel can punch straight through and ruin the chip. The protection is a wrist strap: a band on your wrist, with a cord to a ground point on the bench. It bleeds your charge away steadily, so it never builds up into a spark. In the exam's words, its purpose is to prevent static electricity.

params.title: The wrist strap: the exam answer
items: For the exam: less than 100,000 ohms of resistance
Low enough to drain the charge quickly
Real straps include about 1 megohm in series, for your safety
Connect to a proper ground point, not a water pipe

onScreen: Wrist strap: less than 100,000 ohms (exam answer)
Real straps: about 1 megohm in series
A proper ground point, not a water pipe
scenes.narration: How much resistance should the strap have? For the exam, a wrist strap used when soldering or working with CMOS electronics must have less than 100,000 ohms of resistance, to prevent static electricity. Low resistance lets the charge drain away quickly. Real straps are made differently, though. They include about 1 megohm in series, so that if you touch a live voltage, you aren't solidly connected to ground, and the current through your body stays small. On the test, choose less than 100,000 ohms. The other choices are plainly wrong: a strap can be used with TTL, transistor transistor logic, another family of chips; it connects to a proper ground point, not a water pipe; and it works fine with anti-static floor mats.

params.title: Clearing a plated-through hole
rows: Pulls out molten solder; hole and pads safe

scenes.narration: Strap on, and now the first repair job: removing a part from a plated-through hole. The old solder fills the hole, and all of it has to come out. The preferred method is a vacuum device, either a hand-held solder sucker or a powered desoldering station. You melt the solder, and the vacuum pulls it out of the hole without damaging the copper lining or the pads, the small copper rings around the hole. The trap answers each cause damage. A dental pick can tear the plating. An iron tip hotter than 900 degrees Fahrenheit can lift the pads off the board. And an air jet sprays molten solder across the board.

params.title: The hot gas bonder
items: A stream of heated air or gas melts the solder
Non-contact: no tool touches the part
Suits tiny surface-mount parts

onScreen: Heated air or gas melts the solder
scenes.narration: Melting solder usually means touching it with a hot iron. But some parts are too small or delicate for that, such as the tiny surface-mount parts on modern boards, soldered flat onto the surface instead of through holes. For those, there's the hot gas bonder. It directs a stream of heated air or gas onto the joint, and the solder melts without any tool touching the part. So a hot gas bonder is used for non-contact melting of solder. It's not for applying solder to the iron's tip, not for soldering both sides of a board at once, and not for curing adhesives.

params.title: Removing insulation from wire
rows: Melts the insulation: no blade, no nick
A blade can nick the conductor
A blade can nick the conductor
A blade can nick the conductor

onScreen: Thermal stripper: melts the insulation, no nick
Pocket knife: can nick the conductor
Mechanical stripper: can nick the conductor
Scissor-action tool: can nick the conductor
scenes.narration: Next, wire work. The plastic insulation around a wire has to come off before you can connect it. The ideal method is the thermal stripper, which melts through the insulation with a heated element. There's no blade, so nothing nicks the copper conductor inside. Why does a nick matter? It leaves a thin, weak spot that can snap later from vibration or bending. That's why the pocket knife, the mechanical wire stripper and the scissor action stripping tool are the wrong answers: each one cuts with a blade.

params.title: Cutting plastic wire ties
items: Wire ties: plastic straps that hold wires in bundles
Cut with flush-cut diagonal pliers, and cut flush
Flush: level with the tie's head, so no sharp stub is left
Not semi-flush pliers, scissors or a knife

onScreen: Wire ties hold wires in bundles
Not semi-flush pliers, scissors or a knife
scenes.narration: Once wires are connected, they're bundled neatly with plastic wire ties, straps that loop around the bundle and lock. After a tie is pulled tight, its long tail is cut off. The proper way to cut plastic wire ties is with flush-cut diagonal pliers, and cut flush. Diagonal pliers, or side cutters, have short angled blades, and flush-cut ones leave a smooth, level end. Cut right at the tie's head, and no sharp stub is left to cut hands or scrape nearby insulation. Semi-flush pliers leave a small sharp point, and scissors or a knife can slip and damage the cable.

params.title: Safety first: glasses on
items: Repairing circuit boards: most important is to wear safety glasses
Clipped wire ends fly off the cutters
Molten solder and flux can spatter
An eye injury can't be undone
Holding fixture, solder bridges, dental pick: technique, not safety

onScreen: The other choices are technique, not safety
scenes.narration: Above all the techniques, there's 1 rule that protects you. When repairing circuit board assemblies, the most important thing is to wear safety glasses. Clipped wire ends fly off the cutters at speed. Molten solder can spatter, along with flux, the cleaning chemical inside solder that helps it flow, and so can cleaning solvents. Any of these can hit an eye, and an eye injury can't be undone. The other choices are about technique, not safety: using a holding fixture, a clamp that holds the board, bridging broken tracks with solder, and clearing holes with a dental pick, which, as we saw, can tear the plating. Safety glasses come first.

params.title: Color codes for pair cables
rows: The first pair of the red group

onScreen: Pairs 1–5: white with blue, orange, green, brown, slate
Pairs 6–10: red with the same 5 colors
scenes.narration: Repaired equipment has to be installed properly, so on to installation codes and procedures. In buildings, telephone and data wiring uses pair cables: bundles of wire pairs, each pair twisted together. So that each pair can be told apart, it gets 2 colors. 5 main colors, white, red, black, yellow and violet, each combine with 5 partner colors, blue, orange, green, brown and slate, a grey. 5 times 5 makes 25 pairs. Pairs 1 to 5 are white with each partner in turn. Pair 6 starts the red group, with blue. So in a 25 pair switchboard cable, as found in building telecommunications, the 6th pair color code is red blue, blue red: 1 wire red striped with blue, its partner blue striped with red.

Bigger cables repeat that 25 pair pattern. A 100-pair cable is split into 4 groups of 25 pairs, and each group is wrapped in a colored ribbon called a binder, following the partner colors in order. Pairs 1 to 25 are in the blue binder, 26 to 50 orange, 51 to 75 green, and 76 to 100 brown. So the binder for pairs 51 to 75 is green. Learn the order, blue, orange, green, brown, and you can find any group.

params.title: Routing cables in a vehicle
items: Most important: cables must not interfere with normal vehicle operation
Keep clear of pedals, steering, airbags and seat tracks
Not under floor mats, where they get crushed

onScreen: Most important: don't interfere with the vehicle's normal operation
Clear of pedals, steering, airbags and seat tracks
scenes.narration: In buildings, cables follow color codes. In a vehicle, the big concern is safety. This is a mobile installation: a radio in a car, truck or other vehicle. Cables have to run from the radio to the antenna and the battery, and how you route them matters. The most important thing is assuring that the radio and electronics cables do not interfere with the normal operation of the vehicle. Keep them clear of pedals, steering, airbags, seat tracks and anything hot or moving. A cable snagged in a pedal could cause a crash. Cutting cables to exact length, making the radio reachable from outside, or hiding cables under floor mats, where they get crushed and chafed, are the wrong answers.

params.title: Tie wraps on a radio tower
rows: UV makes the plastic brittle: fails quickly
Carbon black blocks UV: lasts for years

onScreen: White or translucent ties: UV from the Sun destroys them quickly
Black ties: carbon black blocks UV
scenes.narration: From vehicles up to towers. Cables on a radio tower are held with plastic tie wraps, the same kind of wire ties, and their color matters. Don't use white or translucent tie wraps. The reason: UV, ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, deteriorates that plastic very quickly, because ordinary white or clear plastic has nothing in it to block UV. It turns brittle and snaps, and the cables come loose. Black tie wraps contain carbon black, which blocks UV, so they last for years outdoors. The traps offer odd reasons: wasps attracted to white, approval by the FAA, the Federal Aviation Administration, or electrolysis. The real reason is the Sun's UV.

params.title: Standing a rack plumb
items: Plumb: perfectly upright
Check it with a spirit level: a bubble in a tube of liquid
Install a base station rack plumb to just inside the bubble

onScreen: Spirit level: a bubble between 2 marks
Rack plumb to just inside the bubble
scenes.narration: Back down from the tower, inside the equipment room, base station radios, the fixed radios that stay in one place, mount in a tall metal frame called a rack. A rack must stand plumb, meaning perfectly upright, so its weight sits evenly on its base and its doors and equipment hang properly. You check it with a spirit level, a tube of liquid with an air bubble inside, between 2 marks. When the bubble sits just inside the marks, the rack is plumb within practical limits. So a single base station radio rack should be installed plumb to just inside the bubble on a level. Just outside the bubble means it's leaning, and no tolerance at all isn't the answer either.

params.title: SSB tuner to an insulated backstay

callouts.label: Backstay section, cut free by insulators: the antenna
SSB automatic tuner: matches the antenna to the radio
Coax such as RG8U or RG213: radio to tuner only
GTO-15 high-voltage cable: tuner up to the backstay

onScreen: GTO-15 high-voltage cable: tuner to backstay
scenes.narration: Last installation job, on a sailboat. A backstay is the wire rope that braces the mast from the back of the boat. Insulators, which block electricity, near each end cut a section of it free, so that section can serve as the long antenna an HF, high frequency, SSB radio needs. Between them sits an SSB automatic tuner, a box that matches the antenna to the radio on each frequency. Coax runs from the radio to the tuner. But the short lead from the tuner to the backstay feeds the antenna directly and carries very high RF voltage, often thousands of volts, enough to spark through ordinary insulation. So that lead uses GTO-15 high-voltage cable, a heavily insulated single wire. Not RG8U or RG213 coax, and not 16-gauge 2-conductor wire.

params.title: Troubleshooting a 150 W SSB transmitter
labels: Fault: a steady 75 W as soon as the transmitter is keyed
Normal SSB: carrier suppressed, output follows the voice
Probable defect: the carrier is being transmitted

onScreen: Probable defect: the carrier is transmitted
scenes.narration: That SSB radio leads into the last part of the job, troubleshooting: finding out why equipment isn't working right. Know what normal looks like, spot the difference, then reason out the cause. Here's an exam case: a 150 watt marine SSB HF transceiver, a combined transmitter and receiver. You key it, meaning switch it to transmit, and before you say a word, the wattmeter shows a steady 75 watts. Remember, SSB suppresses the carrier, so with no speech the output should be near 0, rising and falling with your voice. A steady output means a carrier is being sent. So there's probably a defect in the system causing the carrier to be transmitted. It's not normal operation, and it isn't a missing sideband or both sidebands being sent.

params.title: Refresher: the capacitor and frequency
items: Capacitor: 2 metal plates separated by an insulator
Blocks steady current
Passes high frequencies easily, low frequencies poorly
Small capacitor: almost a short circuit for RF, nearly invisible to slow signals

onScreen: Small capacitor: a path for RF only
scenes.narration: The next fault needs 1 part explained first: the capacitor. A capacitor is 2 metal plates separated by a thin insulator. Steady current can't cross the gap, but an alternating signal can pass through by charging and discharging the plates, and the faster it alternates, the more easily it passes. A capacitor's opposition to alternating current is called reactance, and it falls as the frequency rises. So a small capacitor acts nearly like a short circuit, an almost free path, for RF, which alternates millions of times a second, while slow signals hardly notice it. That makes it a handy way to drain RF off a wire while leaving a slow signal on that wire alone.

blocks.label: Nearby radio system
blocks.note: Its RF is picked up on the wires

blocks.label: .01 µF capacitor across leads
blocks.note: Bypasses RF without loading the circuit

onScreen: Motor and tachometer leads pick up RF
Add a .01 µF capacitor across the leads
Bypasses RF without loading the circuit
scenes.narration: Now the case. A building's elevator uses a tachometer, a sensor that reports how fast the motor turns. Its wires pick up RF from a nearby radio system, like an antenna. A common fix is to add a .01 microfarad capacitor across the motor and tachometer leads, bridging 1 wire to the other. A microfarad is a millionth of a farad, the unit that measures a capacitor's size, so this is a small one. To RF it's nearly a short circuit, so the RF is drained away, or bypassed, while the slow tachometer signal hardly notices it. It bypasses RF without loading the circuit. A 200 microfarad capacitor is far bigger, so it would pass the slow signal too, loading the circuit heavily. Replacing the tachometer or adding a series resistor doesn't remove the RF.

onScreen: Laptop computer with the maker's software
scenes.narration: Troubleshooting often ends with reprogramming. Modern radios are small computers, and their settings, the channels, tones and features, are loaded into memory. That's called programming. A common method of programming portable or mobile radios is to use a laptop computer, running the maker's programming software, connected to the radio through a programming cable. The trap answers are test equipment, not programming tools: a dummy load, which is a resistor that stands in for an antenna, a wattmeter, and a signal generator.

params.title: Programming without a cable
items: Infra-red communication: a common wireless method
Works like a TV remote control
From a computer interface or from another radio
Not ultraviolet, and not by satellite

onScreen: From a computer interface or another radio
scenes.narration: What if there's no wired connection? Some radios have an infra-red port, a small window that sends and receives invisible light, just like a TV remote control. Programming data can travel that way from a computer interface, or from 1 radio to another. So infra-red communication is a common method to program radios without a wired connection. Watch the trap that swaps in ultraviolet: radios don't program each other with ultraviolet light, and the maker doesn't send programming down by satellite.

params.title: Quick check: the built-in self-test
items: Software-defined transceiver: software does much of the radio's work
Built-in self-test: checks its own circuits and reports faults
The best quick overall evaluation of its condition
No FCC rule forbids self-tests in commercial radios

onScreen: Built-in self-test checks and reports faults
scenes.narration: Some radios take the computer idea further and do most of their work in software. In a software-defined transceiver, jobs that once needed separate circuits, such as filtering and recovering the audio, are done by a computer program. Radios like this usually include a built-in self-test feature that checks the main circuits and reports any faults. For a quick overall evaluation of the radio's operational condition, then, the best way is to use the built-in self-test feature. A full bench check with a spectrum analyzer and service monitor takes far longer. And despite what 1 of the traps claims, no FCC, Federal Communications Commission, rule forbids self-tests in commercial radios.

params.title: DSC on a marine VHF radio

callouts.label: Distress button: sends a digital distress alert
MMSI: the vessel's identity number, entered here

onScreen: Distress button sends a digital alert
scenes.narration: Our last cases come from a boat. A modern marine VHF radio includes DSC, digital selective calling. Instead of a voice call, it sends a short digital message, addressed to 1 particular station or, in an emergency, to every station in range. Press and hold the red distress button, and the radio sends a distress alert that says who you are and where you are. Who you are comes from a number called the MMSI, the Maritime Mobile Service Identity, which works like a phone number for the vessel. Where you are comes from GPS, the Global Positioning System, connected to the back of the radio.

params.title: Checking the GPS connection
items: GPS sends its position as lines of data called sentences
Correct sentence: latitude and longitude appear on the display
No position shown: check the wiring and the sentence format
Never press the distress button to test

onScreen: Verify: latitude and longitude on the display
No position: check wiring and format
Never test with the distress button
scenes.narration: So after connecting the GPS, an installer has to make sure the radio is getting the right data. A GPS receiver sends its position as short lines of text called sentences, in a standard format. Latitude says how far north or south you are, and longitude how far east or west. How do you verify that the correct GPS sentence reaches the DSC radio? Look for latitude and longitude on the display. If they appear, the radio understands the data. If not, check the wiring and the sentence format. Never press the distress button to test it. And the exam's answer isn't a GPS confirmation readout or a position report over the air.

blocks.label: DSC emergency function active
blocks.note: Distress alerts can now be sent

onScreen: The DSC emergency function is activated
Alerts name the vessel, with GPS position
scenes.narration: There's 1 more step before DSC can call for help. Every DSC message identifies the sender by its MMSI, so the distress function stays disabled until a number is entered. The DSC emergency signaling function on a marine VHF is activated by input of a registered 9-digit MMSI. Registered means the number has been officially assigned to that vessel. A GPS input is strongly recommended, so alerts include the position, but it's the MMSI that switches DSC on. A separate 12 volt supply or a second antenna isn't needed. Remember the 9-digit MMSI.

params.title: Key facts to take away
items: Meter movement: 0.05 V for half scale; multiplier for volts, shunt for amps
Oscilloscope: time domain; spectrum analyzer: frequency domain
Receiver sensitivity: 12 dB of SINAD; wideband FM deviation: 5.0 kHz
Wrist strap, for the exam: less than 100,000 ohms
DSC: activated by a registered 9-digit MMSI

onScreen: 0.05 volts; multiplier for volts, shunt for amps
Scope: time domain; analyzer: frequency domain
scenes.narration: Let's wrap up the workbench. Meters run on Ohm's law: half scale on a 50 microampere, 2,000 ohm movement takes 0.05 volts, a series multiplier extends a voltmeter, and a parallel shunt extends an ammeter. The oscilloscope shows signals in the time domain, and the spectrum analyzer in the frequency domain. A receiver's sensitivity is measured at 12 decibels of SINAD, and wideband FM voice deviation tops out at 5.0 kilohertz. For the exam, a wrist strap has less than 100,000 ohms. And a marine DSC radio's emergency function comes alive only when its registered 9-digit MMSI is entered. Now let's check what you remember.
